references.text: The preceding verse provides the context: God will secure justice for his chosen ones. [ref:Luk 18:7|Luke 18:7] promises that God will grant justice to those who cry out to him day and night, and verse 8 confirms this with "he will bring them justice quickly".

[ref:Hab 2:3|Habakkuk 2:3] speaks of the vision (its fulfillment) having its appointed time and hastening toward the end – "if it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay". This connects to Jesus' assurance that God will act swiftly with justice.

[ref:1 Pet 2:6|1 Peter 2:6] quotes Isaiah and speaks of faith: "The one who believes in him will never be put to shame". The question of whether Jesus will find faith on earth relates to the theme of perseverance in faith.

[ref:Heb 10:35-37|Hebrews 10:35-37] exhorts us not to throw away our confidence and quotes Habakkuk: "For yet a little while, and the coming one will come; he will not delay". The theme of patient faith and the Lord's swift coming is the same as in Luke 18:8.

[ref:Luk 17:26-30|Luke 17:26-30] describes the conditions in the days of Noah and Lot, when people were occupied with worldly matters and lacked faith. Jesus' question about whether he will find faith on earth when he comes points back to this warning against spiritual indifference at the coming of the Son of Man.

[ref:Matt 24:12|Matthew 24:12] warns that "because lawlessness will increase, the love of many will grow cold". This sheds light on Jesus' concern in Luke 18:8 about whether he will find faith on earth at his coming.

[ref:Matt 24:44|Matthew 24:44] exhorts the disciples: "Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect". The expression "Son of Man" and his coming directly connect to Luke 18:8.

[ref:2 Tess 2:3|2 Thessalonians 2:3] speaks of the great apostasy that must come before the day of the Lord. Jesus' rhetorical question about whether he will find faith on earth suggests precisely such an apostasy.

[ref:2 Tim 4:1-4|2 Timothy 4:1-4] warns that a time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching but will turn away from the truth. This sheds light on Jesus' concern about the state of faith at his return.

[ref:Åp 6:10|Revelation 6:10] depicts the cry of the martyrs: "Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you judge and avenge our blood?" The theme of God's righteous vengeance and his faithful ones waiting directly connects to the parable of the widow and God's promise to bring justice quickly.

[ref:Jes 59:15-16|Isaiah 59:15-16] describes how truth has vanished and the Lord sees that there is no one to intercede – so he himself intervenes. The parallel to Luke 18:8 is clear: God acts for the sake of justice, but will there be faith among people?

[ref:1 Mos 18:23-32|Genesis 18:23-32] tells of Abraham's intercession for Sodom and the question of whether any righteous people are found there. Jesus' question about whether he will find faith on earth has a similar tone – will there be believing people left?
